newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Indonesian coffee crop seen dipping, trade slow.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian coffee crop seen dipping, trade slow.

text.p: Indonesia's coffee output may dip in the 1997 season, but reports of a sharp fall in production appear unfounded, regional traders said on Wednesday.
Traders who recently conducted preliminary surveys of the crop said heavy rains which pounded Indonesian coffee farms in June-July last year stripped some trees of their flowers.
"The trees are healthy, but they have no flowers on them," a senior dealer for a European commodity house said. "If you have to put a number, it would probably be 10 percent lower."
"I don't think there are any problems with the Indonesian crop," a dealer for a Singapore-based trading house added.
Indonesian traders said earlier this week that domestic prices were firmer because coffee supplies were tight.
"I have been getting reports of a decline in production from several farmers in the Lampung region," one said. "The degree of decline is varied, but the smallest fall was by 10 percent."
Indonesian market sources said last week heavy rains and strong winds had hindered the second flowering of coffee trees and could lead to a fall in the country's output by between 15 to 40 percent.

Another trader here said his company's preliminary estimates of Indonesia's robusta exports this season should range between 300,000 to 310,000 tonnes , slightly down from the more than 320,000 tonnes exported in 1996.
"Some guys don't believe there will be a sharp drop in Indonesia," the trader said.
"You can go into some hills in Sumatra and say the damage looks pretty bad. But it's really too early and we have to get further into the harvest to see how the crop looks like," another dealer said.
Bean supplies remain tight in Indonesia as the bulk of the harvest is not expected to come in until middle to late April.
Prices of Indonesia's benchmark Grade 4, 80 defects, coffee was quoted by the trade at around US$1,400-$1,500 a tonne FOB Lampung port, little changed from last week's $1,450-$1,500.
Business remained slow around the region as volatile markets in London and New York kept most exporters glued to the sidelines, traders said.
"The Vietnamese are shipping out very slowly with prices coming down," a trader said.
"The business is very slow. The regional market is looking for leads," one trader for a Singapore commodity house said.
Dealers said the volume of coffee that has not been committed or sold by Vietnam probably ranges between 60,000 to 80,000 tonnes.

"All of the beans are already off the trees in Dak Lak," a dealer said, refering to the Vietnamese province which produces about two-thirds of the estimated 250,000-270,000 tonnes of robusta coffee exported by the country every season.
Prices of Vietnam's Grade 2, 8.0 percent black and broken, was quoted by regional dealers at about $1,350-$1,420 a tonne FOB Saigon port, down slightly from last week's $1,400-$1,500.
Traders said they feel the London robusta market will be looking for leads when it opens later on Wednesday. Another factor hanging over London is the performance of the arabica market in New York.
"The big question is how much lower New York is going to go," a trader said. "I think London is going to stay in a range between $1,600 and $1,720 (a tonne) basis May."
"London is looking for direction," another dealer said.
The number of lots traded on Tuesday on the Singapore Commodity Exchange (SICOM) reached a paltry 450 lots, unchanged from the total the previous day.

The 150 lots in the May contract was settled at $1,501 a tonne, the 150 lots in the July contract ended at $1,496 a tonne and the last 150 lots in the September contract finished at $1,489 a tonne, SICOM said.
-- Singapore Newsroom (65-8703305)
